lead: This unit shows how to write shell scripts in Bourne shell and Bash, from a one-line command to a small text-processing pipeline. It covers variables, control flow, functions, arguments, files, pipes and the grep/sed/awk tools. You finish able to automate a report from a log or CSV file and to debug the script when it fails.
about: This unit teaches shell scripting as a practical tool. Chapter 3.1 starts with how sh and Bash read a command and run a script. Chapter 3.2 adds variables, quoting and arithmetic; 3.3 uses them in tests, if/case and loops. Chapter 3.4 packs repeated work into functions and reads command-line arguments. Chapter 3.5 connects scripts to files through redirection and file descriptors. Chapter 3.6 chains commands into pipelines, then 3.7 applies grep, sed and awk to real text. Chapter 3.8 closes with exit codes, set options and traps so failures are visible. Each chapter uses small scripts you can run in a lab terminal.

chapters.idea: The shell is both a command interpreter and a programming language; sh is the portable Bourne shell and Bash is its extended successor.
chapters.depth: Cover shell as command interpreter and programming language; sh (Bourne shell, /bin/sh) and Bash (Bourne Again SHell, /bin/bash); interactive use vs script use; first line #!/bin/sh or #!/bin/bash; run as sh file, bash file, or ./file after chmod +x; command lookup for builtins and external programs through PATH; exit status $? where 0 means success. Mention Bash extras such as arrays, [[ ]] and brace expansion, but portable scripts use POSIX sh features. Some syllabi call this shell basics or shell scripting fundamentals.

figure.title: From command to output
figure.aria: A command line passes from the user through shell parsing and command lookup to a kernel process, which writes output to the terminal.

chapters.example: A file greet.sh contains #!/bin/sh on line 1 and echo 'Hi $USER' on line 2. Its permissions are 644. You run ./greet.sh, then chmod 755 greet.sh and run again. State the two outcomes and how bash greet.sh differs.
chapters.trap: The shebang line must be the first line and must give an absolute path; running sh script ignores the shebang, and ./script needs execute permission.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 command-line interface and basic commands
chapters.leave: Leave Unix history and distributions to Unit 1, file permissions to Unit 2, and process control to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Shell variables store strings; quoting decides whether a variable expands, stays literal, or splits into several words.
chapters.depth: Cover shell variables as name=value strings; no spaces around =; read with $NAME or ${NAME}; export to make environment variables; readonly and unset; quoting: single quotes keep text literal, double quotes expand variables and command substitution, backslash escapes one character; command substitution $(cmd) and backticks; arithmetic expansion $((...)) with + - * / %, including integer division; string operators =, !=, -z, -n and numeric operators -eq, -ne, -lt, -le, -gt, -ge; file tests -f, -d, -r, -w, -x as operators used by conditionals. Mention ${VAR:-default} and ${#VAR}. Bash arrays are advanced and only a few universities teach them.

figure.title: Quoting decides expansion
figure.aria: The same stored value is read three ways: double quotes expand it to one word, single quotes keep the text literal, and unquoted expansion may split it on spaces.

chapters.example: After NAME=Asha and COUNT=7, give the output of echo "$NAME has $COUNT"; echo '$NAME has $COUNT'; echo $((COUNT+3)); echo ${#NAME}.
chapters.trap: There must be no spaces around = in NAME=Asha; $COUNT+3 is the string 7+3 unless you use arithmetic expansion, and unquoted variables with spaces split into several words.
chapters.leave: Leave positional parameters to 3.4, test syntax and loops to 3.3, and user environment setup to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Shell control flow makes decisions from exit status: 0 is true or success, non-zero is false or failure; if, case, while, until and for choose which commands run.
chapters.depth: Cover if/then/elif/else/fi, case/esac, while/until/for; for over a word list and C-style for ((i=0; i<5; i++)); while read -r line for files; test [ ] and Bash [[ ]]; exit status rule: 0 true/success, non-zero false/failure; string operators =, !=; numeric -eq, -ne, -lt, -le, -gt, -ge; file tests -f, -d, -r, -w, -x; -z and -n; break and continue. Use counters and simple lists. Some syllabi call this control flow statements and conditional and looping constructs.

figure.title: if/elif/else flow
figure.aria: The first file test succeeds and runs the then block; if it fails, a second directory test runs an elif block or an else error block before the script ends.

chapters.example: A script runs for n in 4 7 10 13; do if (( n % 2 == 1 && n > 5 )); then echo $n; fi; done. Show the output.
chapters.trap: [ $x = 1 ] fails when x is empty unless you quote "$x"; [ $x -eq 1 ] is numeric, while [ $x = 1 ] is string; remember that a shell command's status 0 means true.
chapters.leave: Leave functions and arguments to 3.4, grep/sed/awk to 3.7, and file type details to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Functions group commands inside the same shell and receive their own positional parameters; a function returns an exit status, while data comes back through stdout.
chapters.depth: Cover function definition name() { commands; } and calls name arg1 arg2; functions run in the same shell; local variables in Bash avoid clashes; return sets an exit status from 0 to 255 only, not data; send data back with echo and capture it by result=$(name args); positional parameters $1 to $9 and ${10}, $# count, $0 script name, $@ and $* lists, shift; quote "$@" to keep each argument separate. getopts for options is advanced; only a few universities teach it.

figure.title: Call f 3 5
figure.aria: A main script calls function f with 3 and 5; inside the function $1 is 3 and $2 is 5, the body writes 8 to stdout and returns status 0.

chapters.example: A script has f() { echo $(( $1 + $2 )); return 3; }. It runs f 4 6; s=$?; echo $s. Show the output and explain why the sum cannot be read from the return value.
chapters.trap: return only gives status 0 to 255; $10 means ${1}0, not the tenth argument; unquoted $@ splits arguments that contain spaces, so use "$@".
chapters.leave: Leave file redirection to 3.5, full getopts option parsing to advanced reading, and process exit semantics to 3.8.

chapters.idea: Scripts read and write streams through file descriptors: stdin is 0, stdout is 1 and stderr is 2; redirection and here-documents connect them to files.
chapters.depth: Cover standard streams: stdin fd 0, stdout fd 1, stderr fd 2; redirection >, >>, <, 2>, &>, 2>&1 and /dev/null; here-document <<EOF; read -r line and IFS for fields; while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file; tee to copy a stream; extra descriptors with exec 3<file are advanced and only a few universities teach them. Check exit status after read loops. Some syllabi call this file input and output.

figure.title: Three file descriptors
figure.aria: A script reads data.txt on standard input, sends normal output toward out.txt on file descriptor 1 and errors toward err.txt on file descriptor 2; without redirection both go to the terminal.

chapters.example: A script count.sh runs as ./count.sh < data.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt. data.txt has 3 lines: '1 2', '3 4', '5 6'. The body is while read -r a b; do echo $((a+b)); done. State the contents of out.txt and err.txt and the exit status.
chapters.trap: > truncates the output file before the command reads it; 2>&1 must come after the stdout redirection; read without -r mangles backslashes, and a for loop over cat file breaks names with spaces.
chapters.leave: Leave pipelines to 3.6, text filters to 3.7, and kernel file-descriptor tables to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A pipe sends stdout of one command to stdin of the next, so small filters can be chained into a data-processing pipeline.
chapters.depth: Cover pipe | connecting stdout of the left command to stdin of the right; filters sort, uniq, cut, tr, wc, head, tail, tee, nl; options -d delimiter, -f fields, -k key, -n numeric, -c count; pipeline exit status is the last command; PIPESTATUS and set -o pipefail are Bash and advanced, and only a few universities teach them. Explain that each pipeline stage runs as a separate process, so a variable set inside a stage may not survive in sh.

figure.title: Pipeline for sales.csv
figure.aria: Sales rows are cut to two fields, filtered to Delhi rows, sorted numerically by amount and cut to the first two lines.

chapters.example: sales.csv has 5 lines: Delhi,pen,120; Mumbai,pen,80; Delhi,book,300; Chennai,pen,50; Delhi,book,150. Run cut -d, -f1,3 sales.csv | grep '^Delhi' | sort -t, -k2 -n | head -2. Show the output.
chapters.trap: The pipeline exit status is the last command, so head can hide an earlier grep failure; variables changed inside a pipeline stage do not always survive in the parent sh.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.5 file input and output; Unit 1 basic commands
chapters.leave: Leave grep/sed/awk details to 3.7, redirection details to 3.5, and kernel pipe implementation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: grep finds lines by pattern, sed edits a stream line by line, and awk processes records and fields to select or summarise data.
chapters.depth: Cover grep: basic and extended regex with -E, -i, -v, -n, -c, -l, exit status; sed: s/old/new/g, addresses, -n with p, d, -i with care; awk: pattern { action }, fields $1 to $NF, -F separator, NR and NF, BEGIN/END, printf; print selected columns and sums. Mention egrep is the old form of grep -E. Keep regex to patterns exams use: ^, $, ., *, [], [^], and with -E +, ?, |, (). awk arrays and user functions are advanced; only a few universities teach them.

figure.title: grep to sed to awk
figure.aria: Marks lines pass through grep to drop Ravi, sed changes the space to a comma, and awk keeps scores at least 60 and prints count 3 and sum 229.

chapters.example: marks.txt has 4 lines: 'Asha 78', 'Ravi 45', 'Meena 91', 'Arjun 60'. Run grep -v '^R' marks.txt | sed 's/ /,/' | awk -F, '$2 >= 60 { sum += $2; n++ } END { print n, sum }'. Show the output.
chapters.trap: grep uses regular expressions, not shell globs; sed without g replaces only the first match on each line; awk NR is the record number and NF is the number of fields; $2 compares as a number only when it looks numeric.
chapters.leave: Leave shell loops and variables to 3.2-3.3, pipelines to 3.6, and file permissions for sed -i to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A reliable script checks exit status, stops on defined errors and prints a trace or message so a failure can be found and fixed.
chapters.depth: Cover exit status $? and standard codes: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 misuse, 126 cannot execute, 127 command not found, 128+n killed by signal n. Check with if cmd; then ...; else ...; fi; set -e to stop on error, set -u to stop on an unset variable, set -x to trace commands, set -o pipefail in Bash; trap 'cleanup' EXIT and trap 'handler' ERR; send errors to stderr with >&2; log and exit non-zero. Note that set -e is ignored in some tests and in && or || lists. Some syllabi call this error handling and debugging.

figure.title: Fail fast with set -e
figure.aria: After the first copy succeeds, the second copy fails; with set -e the script exits with status 1, while without set -e it continues, prints done and returns status 0.

chapters.example: backup.sh contains set -e; cp $1 /backup; cp $2 /backup; cp $3 /backup; echo done. Run ./backup.sh a.txt missing.txt c.txt, where missing.txt does not exist. Give the output and exit status with set -e, and without set -e.
chapters.trap: set -e is skipped in commands used by if, while, && or ||; $? is overwritten by the next command, so save it in a variable before testing or printing it.
chapters.leave: Leave process signals and traps at kernel level to Unit 5, process killing to Unit 4, and file permissions to Unit 2.

links: 3.1 shows how a script starts; 3.2 puts values into variables
variables supply test values and loop counters
loops move into functions; functions read arguments
arguments name the files a script reads and writes
redirection and pipes both move streams
pipelines chain grep, sed and awk filters
text filters fail on bad patterns; debugging finds why
